analysis.one_liner: Automatically cancels up to $50,000 in federal student loan debt for each borrower.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Department of Education to automatically cancel up to $50,000 of each borrower's federal student loan debt, wiping out defaulted loans too and removing defaults from credit reports. For one year, every borrower would have been placed in forbearance — no payments due, no interest accruing, and no wage garnishments or collection actions. The canceled debt would not have been taxed as income. Nothing in the bill was ever taken up by a committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal student loan borrowers — roughly 40 million people — including those in default, whose loans would be canceled automatically with no application and no tax bill on the forgiven amount. Borrowers facing wage garnishment would get a one-year pause on collections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal student loan borrowers, including defaulted borrowers

how_it_helps.text: The Department of Education would automatically discharge up to $50,000 of outstanding federal student loan debt per borrower, regardless of repayment status or whether the loan is in default, within 12 months of enactment.
Discharged debt would be excluded from taxable income, so borrowers would not owe a surprise tax bill on the canceled amount.

For one year, all borrowers would be placed in automatic administrative forbearance: no payments due, no interest accruing, and no wage garnishment, Treasury offset, or referral of loans for collection lawsuits.
Borrowers whose defaulted loans were discharged would have the default record removed from their credit history.
Loans would be discharged in descending order of interest rate, so the highest-cost debt would be wiped out first.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of paying off or canceling the discharged loans, since the Department of Education would either assume the obligations or cancel loans it holds — a large one-time federal expense. The government also foregoes future collections on those loans. Members of Congress are explicitly barred from benefiting.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, and the loan servicing industry

drawbacks.text: The discharge is universal — every borrower gets the same up-to-$50,000 regardless of income or need — so the largest dollar benefits would go to borrowers with graduate and professional degrees who typically hold the biggest loan balances, while taxpayers as a whole absorb the cost.
The bill would impose a substantial one-time cost on the federal budget by assuming or canceling outstanding loan obligations and forgoing future collections, with no offsetting revenue in the bill.
The bill itself excludes Members of Congress from eligibility, an acknowledgment that a universal windfall would otherwise flow to officeholders as well as ordinary borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of borrowers carrying federal student debt — including many who defaulted and faced garnishment — the bill offered direct, automatic relief with no application and no tax consequences. The cost is real: a universal $50,000 cancellation is one of the most expensive forms of debt relief, and its universality means a large share of the money would reach relatively high-income borrowers rather than being targeted by need. Whether the tradeoff is worth it depends on how one weighs broad relief against cost and targeting; the bill's exclusion of Members of Congress shows its sponsor was aware of the windfall problem but chose universality anyway.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them ever held a hearing, marked it up, or reported it out, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2021 and referred to three committees — Education and Labor, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — for consideration of the provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the House, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor during the two years the bill was pending.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal government avoided the large cost of a universal debt discharge, and the loan servicing and guaranty industries kept the portfolio of loans they administer; student borrowers received nothing from this bill, though the separate pause on payments and interest that ran from 2020 to 2023 continued under other authorities.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury and loan servicing companies

for.name: Troy Carter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three House committees; it drew no cosponsors and no committee action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup and never reported the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the referral.

against.name: President Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed canceling $50,000 per borrower, saying he supported $10,000 of forgiveness instead, which set the ceiling for what his party pursued.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Publicly stated in 2021 that the President lacked authority to cancel student debt unilaterally and that congressional action would be needed, without putting such a bill on the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no partisan vote — the bill had zero cosponsors from either party and was never brought up, so no party ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and guaranty agencies
industries.note: A mass discharge would erase loans from the portfolio of loans these companies service and administer, eliminating much of the associated servicing revenue. Borrowers gain by having the debt canceled; the companies' income depends on the debt existing.
Taxpayers as a whole would bear the cost of paying off or canceling roughly the loan balances of every federal borrower. The bill provides no offset, so the expense would add to the federal debt.

industries.industry: Private collection agencies for federal student loans
industries.note: The bill bans wage garnishment, Treasury offsets, and referral of loans for collection lawsuits for a year, and the discharge itself would end collection on canceled balances. Their business is collecting on the very debt the bill wipes out.
